title: Computer Organization
description: The CPU, memory, buses and I/O of a computer, memory types and sizes, and the fetch–execute cycle.

study.title: Building blocks of a computer
study.body: A computer consists of a **CPU**, **memory** and **input/output** (I/O) connected by **buses**. The CPU contains the **ALU** (arithmetic and logic operations), the **control unit** (fetches and decodes instructions and directs everything else) and **registers** (fast storage for operands, addresses and results). Memory holds both the program and the data. I/O connects sensors, actuators, displays and keyboards. With **von Neumann** architecture one memory holds instructions and data; **Harvard** architecture has separate instruction and data memories, so both can be accessed at the same time.

study.title: Buses
study.body: A bus is a set of wires that carries several bits at once. The **address bus** (driven by the CPU) selects a memory location or I/O register: $n$ address lines select $2^n$ locations. The **data bus** is bidirectional and carries data and instructions; its width is the number of bits moved per transfer. Devices connect to it through **tristate buffers**, so only one device drives the bus at a time. The **control bus** carries read/write, chip-select, clock and interrupt signals. The graph shows a read cycle: the CPU puts out the address (ADDR valid), pulls $\overline{RD}$ low, and the memory answers with valid data after its access time.

study.title: Memory size and addresses
study.body: Each location usually stores one byte. Sizes use binary prefixes: 1 K = $2^{10}$ = 1024, 1 M = $2^{20}$. A 16-bit address bus spans 0000H to FFFFH (64 K locations). A block of size $S$ starting at address $A$ ends at $A + S - 1$: an 8 K block (8 K = 2000H) starting at 4000H ends at 5FFFH. Memory chips are described as (words) × (bits per word), e.g. 8K × 8.

study.title: Memory types
study.body: **RAM** (read/write) is volatile: **SRAM** stores bits in flip-flops (fast, simple, larger cells); **DRAM** stores charge on a capacitor (dense and cheap, but must be **refreshed** every few ms). **ROM** is non-volatile: mask ROM (written at manufacture), PROM (written once), EPROM (UV-erasable), **EEPROM** (electrically erasable, byte by byte, slow writes). **Flash** is non-volatile and erased in blocks, with a limited number of write cycles. A microcontroller keeps its program in flash/ROM and its variables in SRAM.

study.title: The fetch–execute cycle
study.body: The **program counter** (PC) holds the address of the next instruction. Each cycle the CPU puts the PC on the address bus, reads the instruction into the **instruction register**, advances the PC, decodes the instruction, fetches any operands, lets the ALU execute it and writes the result back (to a register or memory). Then it repeats. A jump or branch simply loads a new value into the PC. The execution time of a program follows from the number of instructions, the average clock cycles per instruction (CPI) and the clock frequency.

steps.title: CPU, memory and I/O
steps.body: Every computer, from a laptop to the controller in a washing machine, has the same structure: a **CPU** that executes instructions, **memory** that stores the program and data, and **I/O** that connects it to the outside world. They are connected by three **buses**: address, data and control.

steps.prompt: Match each part of a computer to its job.
pairs: Adds, compares and does logic on data
Wires that carry several bits at once
steps.explanation: The CPU is the ALU plus the control unit (plus registers). The control unit fetches each instruction from memory, decodes it and sets up the ALU, memory and I/O. Buses connect all of them.

steps.title: Three buses
steps.body: The CPU sends an address on the **address bus** to select one memory location or I/O register. With $n$ address lines it can select $2^n$ different addresses. The **data bus** carries the data in either direction. The **control bus** says what should happen: read or write, which chip is selected, and when (clock).

steps.prompt: A small processor has {{n}} address lines and one byte per address. How many memory locations can it address? Give the exact number.
steps.explanation: Each address line doubles the number of combinations: $2^{ {{n}} }$ = **{{2^n||5}}** locations = {{2^(n-10)}} K (with 1 K = 1024).

steps.prompt: Which bus carries information in **both** directions between the CPU and memory?
steps.explanation: Data flows from memory to the CPU on a read and from the CPU to memory on a write, so the data bus is bidirectional. Addresses are always produced by the CPU, so the address bus is one-way.

steps.prompt: Two devices may put data on the shared data bus at the same time, as long as they send the same number of bits.
steps.explanation: False. Only one device may drive the bus at a time, otherwise their outputs fight (bus contention). Every device connects through **tristate buffers**; the control signals enable the buffers of only the device that is sending, all others are in the high-impedance (open-switch) state.

steps.title: Fetch, decode, execute
steps.body: The **program counter** (PC) holds the address of the next instruction. The CPU repeats a simple cycle: put the PC on the address bus and read the instruction into the **instruction register** (fetch), advance the PC, work out what the instruction means (decode), and carry it out (execute), possibly reading or writing memory. A jump just loads a new address into the PC.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of executing one instruction in order.
items: Put the PC on the address bus
Read the instruction into the instruction register
Advance the PC to the next instruction
Execute it and store the result
steps.explanation: Fetch (PC onto the address bus, instruction into the IR, PC advanced), then decode, then execute and write back. Advancing the PC right after the fetch means it already points at the next instruction while the current one executes.

steps.prompt: Which type of memory loses its contents when the power is switched off?
steps.explanation: RAM (static or dynamic) is **volatile**: SRAM flip-flops and DRAM capacitors lose their state without power. ROM, EEPROM and flash are non-volatile, which is why programs and settings that must survive power-off are stored there.

steps.prompt: A byte-organised memory has a capacity of {{2^(k-10)||4}} Kbytes (1 K = 1024). How many address lines does it need?
How many **bits** can be stored in a {{N}}-Kbyte memory (1 K = 1024)?
A {{4*m}}-Kbyte RAM chip is mapped into a 16-bit address space, starting at address {{s}}000H. What is the **last** address it occupies?
steps.explanation: {{4*m}} K = {{4096*m||5}} bytes = {{m}}000H. The last address is start + size − 1 = {{s}}000H + {{m}}000H − 1 = **{{s+m-1}}FFFH**. ({{s+m}}000H is the first address **after** the chip.)

steps.prompt: A {{T}}-Kbyte memory (8-bit words) is built from {{c}}K × {{w}} memory chips. How many chips are needed?
steps.explanation: Depth: {{T}} K / {{c}} K = {{T/c}} chips are needed to get enough locations. Width: 8 bits / {{w}} bits = {{8/w}} chips side by side to form one byte. Total: {{T/c}} × {{8/w}} = **{{T*8/(c*w)}}** chips.

steps.prompt: A data bus is {{w}} bits wide and makes one transfer per clock cycle at {{f|Hz}}. What is its maximum data rate in bytes per second?
steps.explanation: Each transfer moves {{w}} bits = {{w/8}} bytes. Rate = {{w/8}} B × {{f|Hz}} = **{{w/8*f|B/s}}**.

steps.prompt: The timing diagram shows a memory read cycle on a 50 MHz bus. ADDR and DATA are high while the address and the data on the bus are valid; $\overline{RD}$ is the active-low read strobe. What is the access time of the memory (from valid address to valid data)?
steps.explanation: The address becomes valid at $t$ = 10 ns and the data at $t$ = {{10+tacc}} ns, so $t_{acc}$ = {{10+tacc}} − 10 = **{{tacc}} ns**. The CPU samples the data at the end of the read strobe ($t$ = 90 ns), so the memory must have an access time below 80 ns here; a slower memory would need extra wait states.

steps.prompt: A program executes {{N}} instructions with an average of {{cpi}} clock cycles per instruction on a {{f|Hz}} processor. How long does it take?
steps.explanation: $t = N \cdot \text{CPI} / f$ = {{N}} × {{cpi}} / {{f|Hz}} = {{N*cpi}} cycles × {{1/f|s}} = **{{N*cpi/f|s}}**.

steps.prompt: Match each memory type to its description.
pairs: Contents fixed when the chip is made
steps.explanation: SRAM and DRAM are both volatile; DRAM is denser but must be refreshed because the charge leaks away. Flash and mask ROM are non-volatile: flash can be rewritten in blocks (a limited number of times), mask ROM never.

steps.prompt: In a microwave-oven controller, where should the cooking time that the user has just typed in be stored while the oven runs?
steps.explanation: The value changes often and only needs to exist while the oven is on, so fast read/write RAM is the right place (SRAM, as used inside microcontrollers). ROM and EPROM cannot simply be written by the program, and a hard disk is far too slow, large and expensive for this.

steps.prompt: A CPU with a 16-bit address bus uses memory chips of {{2^(k-10)}} Kbytes each.

ask.prompt: How many of the address lines go to the address inputs of each chip?
ask.explanation: {{2^(k-10)}} K = $2^{ {{k}} }$ locations, so each chip needs the **{{k}}** lowest address lines $A_0$–$A_{ {{k-1}} }$.

ask.prompt: How many upper address lines are left to decode which chip is selected?
ask.explanation: The chip uses $A_0$–$A_{ {{k-1}} }$ ({{k}} lines). The remaining 16 − {{k}} = **{{16-k}}** lines ($A_{ {{k}} }$–$A_{15}$) feed the address decoder, which can select up to $2^{ {{16-k}} }$ = {{2^(16-k)}} chips.

steps.prompt: A 16 K memory chip is selected when $A_{15}$ = {{a15}} and $A_{14}$ = {{a14}}; $A_0$–$A_{13}$ go to the chip. Which address range does it occupy?
steps.explanation: The top hex digit holds $A_{15}A_{14}A_{13}A_{12}$. With $A_{15}A_{14}$ = {{a15}}{{a14}} and the lower 14 bits running from all 0s to all 1s, the address goes from {{a15}}{{a14}}00 0000 0000 0000 to {{a15}}{{a14}}11 1111 1111 1111. Each combination of the two top bits selects one quarter (16 K = 4000H) of the 64 K space.

steps.prompt: The PC contains 0100H. The CPU executes three instructions that are {{l1}}, {{l2}} and {{l3}} bytes long (no jumps). What does the PC contain afterwards?
steps.explanation: The PC advances by the **length in bytes** of each instruction it fetches, not by 1 per instruction: 0100H + {{l1}} + {{l2}} + {{l3}} = **010{{l1+l2+l3}}H**. It then points at the first byte of the fourth instruction.

steps.prompt: A loop of {{n}} instructions (average CPI = {{cpi}}) runs {{R}} times on a {{f|Hz}} microcontroller. How long does the loop take?
steps.explanation: Cycles = {{R}} × {{n}} × {{cpi}} = {{R*n*cpi}}. Time = cycles / $f$ = {{R*n*cpi}} / {{f|Hz}} = **{{R*n*cpi/f|s}}**.

steps.prompt: A DDR memory module has a 64-bit data bus with an I/O clock of {{f|Hz}} and transfers data on **both** clock edges. What is its peak data rate in bytes per second?
steps.explanation: 64 bits = 8 bytes per transfer, 2 transfers per clock cycle: 8 B × 2 × {{f|Hz}} = **{{16*f|B/s}}**. (Forgetting the double data rate gives half that.)

steps.prompt: Which architecture lets the CPU fetch the next instruction and read a data operand in the **same** clock cycle?
options: Harvard (separate instruction and data memories and buses)
Von Neumann (one memory for instructions and data)
steps.explanation: With one shared memory and bus (von Neumann), instruction fetches and data accesses must take turns: the 'von Neumann bottleneck'. Harvard architecture, used in many microcontrollers and DSPs, has two separate paths, so both can happen at once.

steps.prompt: With memory-mapped I/O, the program reads an input port with the same load instruction it uses to read a memory location.
steps.explanation: True. Memory-mapped I/O gives every I/O register an address in the normal memory space, so ordinary load and store instructions access it. The address decoder routes those particular addresses to the I/O device instead of to memory.

steps.prompt: A DRAM has {{R||4}} rows, and every row must be refreshed at least once every {{T|s}}. If the refreshes are spread evenly, how often must a row-refresh command be issued (time between commands)?
steps.explanation: {{R||4}} refreshes must fit in {{T|s}}: $t = T/R$ = {{T|s}} / {{R||4}} = **{{T/R|s}}**. The memory controller inserts these refresh cycles automatically; this is the price DRAM pays for its tiny capacitor cells.
